messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amara is a 42-year-old Ethiopian-American woman who works as a train conductor for a regional rail line. She is married and lives with her husband in a mid-sized city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that her husband described as having rendered her "unreachable." Her PCL-5 score of 44 places her in the clinically significant range for PTSD, and what emerges across the intake and early sessions is a presentation shaped almost entirely by a period of political detention she survived in her early thirties, before her immigration to the United States.

Amara was held for several weeks by state security forces following a political gathering she had attended. During that time she was subjected to repeated sessions of physical torture in a room she described, haltingly, as smelling of burning — something electrical, she thought, or perhaps cloth. The silences between sessions were, in her telling, the worst part: long stretches of absolute quiet in which she could not know what was coming, punctuated by the sudden movements of guards entering without warning. She was beaten, and she watched others be beaten. She remembers the wounds on their bodies with a vividness she cannot explain and cannot fully bear.

What Amara carries now is not a story she can tell. She has fragments — images, mostly: a particular angle of light, a pattern of bruising on a forearm, the shape of a doorframe. She cannot assemble these into a coherent narrative even when she tries alone at night, and she has come to believe this means something is fundamentally wrong with her mind. What makes these fragments so dangerous is that they do not feel like memories. When they surface, Amara is certain — in her body, in her chest and her hands — that it is happening again, right now. This quality of reliving is what first made her afraid to go to work.

She is a train conductor, and the job is full of the things that undo her. The tunnels bring sudden, complete silence before a station announcement cuts through — and in that silence, her body floods with the same formless dread that preceded each session in detention. The smell of smoke from a track fire or a passenger's clothing can arrive without warning, and within seconds she is no longer on the train. Visible injuries on passengers — a scraped hand, a bandaged arm — pull her eyes involuntarily and send fragmentary images cascading. These triggers do not simply distress her; they return her to the memory, and the memory, once activated, sharpens every threat in her environment. After a trigger, she cannot stop scanning. She listens for sounds at the doors between carriages. She watches for sudden movements from passengers rising from their seats, and when someone stands quickly she is on guard before she has consciously registered it.

The strategies Amara has developed to manage this have become a second architecture of suffering. She smokes now — something she never did before — and she is aware, without being able to stop, that she reaches for a cigarette most urgently after a moment of sensory alarm on the train. She has developed a habit of checking her own body throughout the day, running her hands along her arms and ribs as though verifying she is intact, a behaviour that began as reassurance and has become a ritual that keeps her attention fastened to physical threat. She also rehearses catastrophes mentally before each shift: the train derailing, a passenger attacking her, a fire in the carriage. She believes this preparation will protect her, but the rehearsal itself fills her mind with images that reactivate the same fragmentary memories she is trying to manage, and those memories, once stirred, leave her hypervigilant and unable to relax for the remainder of the day. She cannot unwind at home either. Her husband has noticed that she listens at night for sounds of entry, that she startles at his movements in the kitchen, that she is present in body but somewhere else entirely.

What finally brought Amara to seek help was a shift last autumn in which she froze on the platform during a routine stop, unable to move or speak for nearly two minutes after a passenger walked past trailing the smell of smoke. A supervisor filed an incident report. Amara is afraid, above everything, that she is losing her ability to do the work that anchors her life in this country. What she hopes for, she said quietly in the first session, is to be able to tell herself what happened — to have it be a story with a past tense.
